segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The Western has been one of Hollywood's staple products since the dawn of cinema. It is undoubtedly the most American of genres, but not always the most acclaimed. Perhaps because they could be produced quickly and on low budgets - the landscape was ready-made and real cowboys were willing to work as extras - Westerns were often dismissed as "pastime" entertainment.

segments.original: In the silent era, pioneers such as Allan Dwan (1885-1981) and Raoul Walsh (1887-1980) often turned out one film a week, from screenplay to final cut. In 1909, the Bison studio arrived in California; in 1910, Broncho Billy Anderson became the first Western star. According to film historian Ed Buscombe's calculations, 213 of the 1,001 American films made that year were Westerns. With the arrival of sound, the genre's popularity declined somewhat, although Western production fell only slightly until the 1960s. Hollywood made more than 800 films in the genre in the 1950s.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Stagecoach (1939), by John Ford (1894-1973), marks the beginning of a period in which Westerns were directed by major filmmakers, such as Ford himself (returning to the genre after more than 10 years away), Michael Curtiz (1886-1962), Fritz Lang (1890-1976) and Howard Hawks (1896-1977), who created famous classics such as Red River (1948) and Rio Bravo (1959).

tracks.title: The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The Western is Hollywood's most easily recognizable genre. The James gang in The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford (2007) and the bandits in The Great Train Robbery (1903) wear different hats, but their looks and attitudes clearly identify them as belonging to the same genre.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Westerns are almost always associated with a specific place and historical period: west of the Mississippi River, south of the 49th parallel, north of the Rio Grande, and sometime between 1865 (the end of the American Civil War) and 1890 (when the census declared that the Frontier no longer existed).

segments.original: For some, the Western is a narrative that can be set in Texas, in Vietnam or in outer space: Outland (1981) transposes High Noon (1952) to one of Jupiter's moons. Even so, the set of historical events, characters and places remains at its core.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The Western both celebrates and rewrites the history of the United States. John Ford, the best-known director of Westerns, said that his portrayal of the gunfight at the O.K. Corral in Tombstone, Arizona, in My Darling Clementine (1946), was drawn directly from the account given by Wyatt Earp himself. That story - like the stories of many other Westerns that claim to be based on true events - is debatable; it is said that Westerns are not so much about the West as about other Westerns.

tracks.title: Learn more: John Ford and Racism

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Learn more: John Ford and Racism.
segments.text: Learn more: John Ford and Racism.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Ford became sympathetic to Native Americans and African Americans late in his career, but he always had to defend himself against accusations of racism. Ethan is not the only racist in The Searchers (1956). Laurie, desperate for Martin to give up his search for Debbie, is equally virulent: "Fetch what home? The leavings of Comanche bucks, sold time and again to the highest bidder, with savage brats of her own?" Being part Cherokee, Martin is apparently more tolerant of interracial mixing. But when his Native American wife (Beulah Archuletta) lies down beside him, he pushes her away. The sadness Martin expresses when she is found dead by the cavalry does not soften the cruelty that the character - and Ford - inflicts on her.

segments.original: Given the weight the myth of the Last Frontier carries in the American psyche, this kind of revisionism is to be expected. Sometimes the process itself becomes the subject of Westerns, whether in iconoclastic films such as Black Patch (1957), by Allen H. Miner (1917-2004), or Ford's own The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance (1962), famous for the line "This is the West, sir. When the legend becomes fact, print the legend".

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Like Altman, Ford knew that the Western was a manufactured legend, but unlike him, Ford saw this in positive terms: only in The Searchers (1956) did he properly explore the dark side of the Western hero. In the late 1930s and early 1940s, the dominant tone of Westerns was one of affirmation mixed with a certain nostalgia.

segments.original: Ford's My Darling Clementine shows Wyatt Earp (Henry Fonda) arriving in Tombstone and leaving behind a town where cattle rustlers and drunken Indians have been replaced by a church and a school. Shane (1953) offers a more self-critical version of the arrival of the gunfighter with a dark past who rids the town of villainy before returning to the wilderness.

segments.original: Less affirmative Westerns marked the 1940s and especially the 1950s. Written by screenwriter Carl Foreman, who would soon be added to the FBI's blacklist. Other blacklisted writers who worked on Westerns include Albert Maltz and Ben Maddow, who wrote Broken Arrow (1950) and Johnny Guitar (1954), respectively. Broken Arrow is an early example of a more sympathetic portrayal of Native Americans, as also seen in Apache (1954).

segments.original: The "psychological Western" became another hallmark of the postwar period. Pursued (1947), by Raoul Walsh, features a Robert Mitchum haunted by his past in a dark, noir-style landscape. Paul Newman is an unbalanced Billy the Kid in The Left Handed Gun (1958), and in The Gunfighter (1950) Gregory Peck plays a man pursued by his own reputation as the "fastest gun", knowing that some ambitious young man will turn up to take his place.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The Hollywood Western survived into the 1960s and beyond, driven by a new generation of directors who moved from television into the film industry, among them Robert Altman, Arthur Penn (1922-2010) and Sam Peckinpah (1925-1984). Peckinpah was particularly important for passionately revisiting some Western traditions, as in Ride the High Country (1962), and more violently in The Wild Bunch (1969) and Pat Garrett & Billy the Kid (1973).

segments.original: The genre even survived the box office failure of Heaven's Gate (1980). Hollywood took a break, but went on producing teen Westerns, Westerns with gay themes and, in 2007, a remake of 3:10 to Yuma (1957), the kind of efficient combination of outlaw characters and landscape that became characteristic of 1950s films.
